title: Two loaves
hookLine: two loaves recall the double manna; they stay covered while the wine is blessed

cards: Friday morning, a bakery in a Jewish neighborhood. The loaves are stacked up: shiny, golden, braided, soft inside, a little sweet. Customer after customer asks for two, and by noon the shelves are nearly bare.

On the Friday night table there's another odd detail: the loaves sit under a cloth, often embroidered, sometimes made by a child at school, while the wine is blessed. Two loaves, under a cloth, waiting their turn.

teach.h: TWO LOAVES FOR THE DOUBLE MANNA.
teach.b: Why two? Go back to the manna, a few days ago on this path. Every morning in the wilderness, bread from heaven, enough for one day.
But on the sixth day, the Torah says, the people gathered twice as much, a double portion, because nothing would fall on Shabbat.
So the Shabbat table has two loaves, lechem mishneh, double bread, to remember the double manna. Two loaves say: there was enough, even for the day nobody gathered. Now the name.
In the Torah, challah is actually the portion of dough set aside for the priests.
Some bakers still pinch off a small piece of dough and set it aside before baking, with a blessing, and the whole loaf came to be called by that name. The braids are a custom, not a law.
They're common among Ashkenazi Jews, whose families came from central and eastern Europe; other communities bake flat breads or round loaves, and round loaves are a New Year custom. Why the cloth?
One says the manna lay between two layers of dew, one below and one above, so the bread sits on a board and under a cover.
Another is so gentle it's told as a children's story too: normally bread's blessing comes first, so the bread is covered so it won't be embarrassed while the wine goes ahead of it.

The lesson people draw: if even a loaf's feelings count, so does everyone's at the table. Then the cover comes off, the blessing is said, and the bread, often sprinkled with salt, is torn and passed around.

how: At Shabbat meals, two loaves of challah sit covered on the table during Kiddush; then the cover is removed, the blessing over bread is said, and the challah is often salted, torn and shared.

games.q: you're setting the Shabbat table. the wine will be blessed first, but the bread's blessing usually comes first. what do you do with the challah?
o: put it away until after Kiddush.
games.why: it's covered: one reason is the dew over the manna, another that the bread shouldn't be 'embarrassed' while the wine goes first.

practice: Picture your next meal with a napkin laid over the bread, or over whatever is on the plate.

Think about where it came from, the field, the bakery, the hands, the truck, and one way you had enough this week, even when you didn't do the gathering. Then picture lifting the cloth slowly, like opening a gift.

orig.note: Hebrew: challah, first the portion of dough given to the priests, then the name of the Shabbat loaf.
